readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — “Think me—for a change—bad!” (Chapter XI)
readings.challenge: Notice how the governess sets a trap for Miles, and how she ends up caught in it herself.
readings.focus: Miles explains his midnight walk, and his explanation leaves no way behind it.
readings.context: The Turn of the Screw (1898), by Henry James, is the written account of a young governess, set down years afterwards, of her charge of two orphaned children, Miles and Flora, at Bly, a country house in England, for their uncle in London, who made her promise never to trouble him about them. In the chapters before this one she has come to believe that two figures she has seen about the house are Peter Quint, the master’s valet, and Miss Jessel, the governess before her, both now dead, as the housekeeper, Mrs. Grose, identified them; she believes too that the children see them and hide it. Miles has been sent home from school without a reason given. The night before this chapter she found Flora looking out of her window and then saw Miles standing on the lawn at midnight, looking up toward the tower above her. The long dash ——— marks a sentence broken off. The back of the tapestry is the hidden side of a thing; a cleft stick, a trap with no way out; to go unhung, to escape hanging.
readings.contentNote: Psychological dread, and a governess’s fierce watching of a child.

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XI, the whole chapter; opens “It was not till late next day that I spoke to Mrs. Grose; the rigour with which I kept my…”; closes “…of all the reserves of goodness that, for his joke, he had been able to draw upon.”.

questions.prompt: The governess calls Mrs. Grose “a magnificent monument to the blessing of a want of imagination.” What does she value in the housekeeper, and what does the phrase reveal about the narrator?
facilitatorNotes: Mrs. Grose believes her “absolutely,” and her calm face will give nothing away to the servants. She offers her mind as she would offer a clean saucepan for a witch’s broth: she receives without judging. The narrator is grateful and condescending at once. Readers who doubt the governess notice that her only confidante is one she praises for lacking imagination.
evidence: She believed me, I was sure, absolutely:
she was a magnificent monument to the blessing of a want of imagination,
she would have held out a large clean saucepan.

questions.prompt: Why can’t the governess simply ask Miles whether he has seen Quint? What does she fear would happen if she named what she suspects?
facilitatorNotes: Those who look after children are condemned for filling them with “superstitions and fears”; if she were the first to name the dead and was wrong, no one would forgive her. So the boy “had” her: whatever he does, she must not speak first. The whole novel turns on this unsaid name.
evidence: so long as I should continue to defer to the old tradition of the criminality of those caretakers of the young who minister to superstitions and fears.
if, by the faintest tremor of an overture, I were the first to introduce into our perfect intercourse an element so dire?

questions.prompt: Miles says he went out so that she would “Think me—for a change—bad!” Is this a confession, an evasion, or a joke? How does the governess take it?
facilitatorNotes: As a joke it is perfect: a good boy playing at being bad, sealed with a kiss. She says it was exactly the account that left her least room to look behind it, and she is both moved and beaten (“practically the end of everything”). A reader can take it as a clever child’s prank or as a practised evasion; the text supports both.
evidence: Think me—for a change—bad!
He had given exactly the account of himself that permitted least of my going behind it,
When I’m bad I am bad!

questions.prompt: “It was I who fell into the trap!” What trap? Does Miles’s arrangement with Flora confirm the governess’s fears or explain the night innocently?
facilitatorNotes: Miles says he arranged for Flora to wake and look out, so that the governess would look too and see him. It gives a natural account of Flora at the window the night before. It also shows the children planning together behind her back, which is what she fears. The last sentence, about “all the reserves of goodness” he drew on “for his joke,” can be read as sincere or as irony.
evidence: Oh, I arranged that with Flora.
It was I who fell into the trap!
my recognition of all the reserves of goodness that, for his joke, he had been able to draw upon.

readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — “They’re his and they’re hers!” (Chapter XII)
readings.challenge: Separate what the governess has seen from what she concludes, and listen to how Mrs. Grose answers.
readings.focus: The governess’s theory of the children, and the uncle no one may call.
readings.context: Recap: The governess caught Miles out on the lawn at midnight; he told her, with a kiss, that he had gone out only so that she would think him bad for a change, and that he had arranged for Flora to wake and look out. The next afternoon she tells Mrs. Grose about it while the children walk on the lawn below. In earlier chapters Mrs. Grose told her that Quint had been too free with the boy and that he and Miss Jessel were together in a way she thought shameful. The long dash ——— marks a sentence broken off. Laws! is a country exclamation, Lord!; a brace is a pair.
readings.contentNote: Talk of children corrupted by dead servants who, the governess says, want to destroy them.

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XII, the whole chapter; opens “The particular impression I had received proved in the morning light, I repeat, not quite…”; closes ““I would leave, on the spot, both him and you.””.

questions.prompt: “It’s a game... it’s a policy and a fraud!” How does the governess turn the children’s beauty and goodness into evidence against them? Is the reasoning sound?
facilitatorNotes: Their goodness is “unnatural”; they are not good but “absent,” living a life of their own with the dead; their silence about Quint and Miss Jessel proves they meet. Whatever the children do confirms the theory, so nothing could disprove it. That is a weakness in reasoning; within the story, though, she may still be right.
evidence: Their more than earthly beauty, their absolutely unnatural goodness.
They haven’t been good—they’ve only been absent.
it would be made so by the systematic silence of each.

questions.prompt: “I go on, I know, as if I were crazy; and it’s a wonder I’m not.” Why does the governess raise the question of her own sanity, and what does she claim instead?
facilitatorNotes: She anticipates the objection before Mrs. Grose can make it, and answers that what she has seen has made her “more lucid.” She admits her lucidity “must have seemed awful.” The narrator puts the question of her own reliability in front of the reader and leaves it there.
evidence: I go on, I know, as if I were crazy; and it’s a wonder I’m not.
it has only made me more lucid,
My lucidity must have seemed awful,

questions.prompt: Where, according to the governess, are the dead seen, and what does she think they want? What exactly does Mrs. Grose accept?
facilitatorNotes: Always at a distance and at an edge: towers, roofs, windows, the far side of pools. They want to draw the children across that distance, to come to them and “perish in the attempt.” Mrs. Grose accepts that Quint and Miss Jessel were “rascals” in life; her memory supports the depravity, but she asks what they “can now do,” which is the whole question.
evidence: the top of towers, the roof of houses, the outside of windows, the further edge of pools;
And perish in the attempt!
They were rascals! But what can they now do?

questions.prompt: Why won’t the governess write to the children’s uncle, and why does she threaten to leave if Mrs. Grose does? What does the threat reveal?
facilitatorNotes: She promised to give him no worry and is proud of keeping her terms; a letter would make her look mad or, worse, look like a scheme to draw his attention to her “slighted charms.” The threat shows how much her feeling for the absent master governs her, even more than the children’s danger. It also leaves Bly without any adult outside it who knows.
evidence: That’s charming news to be sent him by a governess whose prime undertaking was to give him no worry.
the fine machinery I had set in motion to attract his attention to my slighted charms.
I would leave, on the spot, both him and you.

readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — the prodigious hushes (Chapter XIII)
readings.challenge: Read for what is never said: list the subjects the governess and the children avoid, and how they avoid them.
readings.focus: A month in which everything is talked about except the dead.
readings.context: Recap: The governess has told Mrs. Grose her theory: the children’s goodness is a fraud, and they belong to Quint and Miss Jessel, who want to draw them to destruction. Mrs. Grose begged her to send for the children’s uncle; she refused, and threatened to leave if Mrs. Grose appealed to him. Since the night she glimpsed a woman at the foot of the stair she has seen nothing more. “All roads lead to Rome” is a proverb: every path ends in the same place. A mot is a witty saying; Harley Street, a street of fine houses in London.

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XIII, the whole chapter; opens “It was all very well to join them, but speaking to them proved quite as much as ever an…”; closes “…a thunderstorm to a day of suffocation. It was at least change, and it came with a rush.”.

questions.prompt: The governess says the children were “aware of my predicament.” What signs of their awareness does she give? Could they be read another way?
facilitatorNotes: Conversations swerve away from “forbidden ground,” doors are shut “with a little bang,” and the children ask endlessly about her own family and village. She even imagines one child nudging the other. But the nudge is her invention, and children who love stories about a governess’s home need no secret motive. The paragraph lets us see the evidence and the interpretation at once.
evidence: There were days when I could have sworn that one of them had, with a small invisible nudge, said to the other:
They pulled with an art of their own the strings of my invention and my memory;

questions.prompt: “Well, my eyes were sealed, it appeared, at present.” Why is the governess not relieved to see nothing? What does she fear more than seeing?
facilitatorNotes: She wants “the fulness of my own exposure”: to see whatever the children see. What frightens her is that her eyes may be closed just when theirs are open, so that the visits go on without her. Seeing has become her protection, and her purpose.
evidence: I greatly preferred, as a safeguard, the fulness of my own exposure.
my eyes might be sealed just while theirs were most opened.

questions.prompt: Autumn at Bly is “like a theatre after the performance—all strewn with crumpled playbills.” What does the image suggest about the place and about the governess?
facilitatorNotes: The summer’s apparitions were a show; now the stage is empty and she waits for the next one, recognising the “signs” and “the moment, the spot.” The image makes Bly a stage and the governess an audience, or a performer. Readers can ask whether the drama is happening at Bly or in the way she watches it.
evidence: was like a theatre after the performance—all strewn with crumpled playbills.
I recognised the signs, the portents—I recognised the moment, the spot.

questions.prompt: What are the “prodigious, palpable hushes,” and why does the governess still refuse to speak the names? What does she do with the children’s letters to their uncle?
facilitatorNotes: They are sudden stillnesses inside ordinary noise, when she feels “the outsiders” are there. She will not name the dead, since the children “have the manners to be silent” and speaking would be base. Meanwhile she keeps their letters, unposted, “to this hour.” She calls it keeping her promise; a reader may see a governess who controls every line between the children and the world.
evidence: one of our prodigious, palpable hushes occurred
They have the manners to be silent, and you, trusted as you are, the baseness to speak!
They were too beautiful to be posted; I kept them myself;

readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — “I want my own sort!” (Chapter XIV)
readings.challenge: Follow the walk to church line by line: who leads, who answers, and who gains ground.
readings.focus: Miles asks when he is going back to school, and the governess loses an argument she cannot afford to have.
readings.context: Recap: For a month the governess and the children lived in a silence about the dead that she believed the children shared and enjoyed; she saw no apparitions but felt them in sudden hushes. The children kept asking when their uncle would come, and she kept their letters to him unposted. The long dash ——— marks a sentence broken off. A gaoler is a jailer; a hassock, a cushion to kneel on; the last act and the catastrophe are terms of the theatre.

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XIV, the whole chapter; opens “Walking to church a certain Sunday morning, I had little Miles at my side and his sister,…”; closes “…gave me another look charged with that expression and then marched off alone into church.”.

questions.prompt: The governess calls Miles’s question “a revolution” and says the curtain rose “on the last act of my dreadful drama.” Why does a simple question about school feel so large to her?
facilitatorNotes: School means the unexplained expulsion, and behind it, for her, everything she fears. The question also ends the children’s “magnificent little surrender” to her constant company: she has been, in her own word, a gaoler. For the first time Miles asks for something openly, and the asking itself is the challenge.
evidence: when in the world, please, am I going back to school?
I was like a gaoler with an eye to possible surprises and escapes.
the curtain rose on the last act of my dreadful drama

questions.prompt: What does Miles say he wants, in his own words? Are these the wishes of an ordinary boy?
facilitatorNotes: Not to be always with a lady; to “see more life”; his “own sort,” meaning boys. Many readers hear nothing but a bright boy chafing at a governess’s company, which is what he says. The governess hears hints in everything, and the dialogue lets both readings stand.
evidence: You know, my dear, that for a fellow to be with a lady always———!
Well—I want to see more life.
I want my own sort!

questions.prompt: Miles himself brings up “that one night.” Why might he, and what does the governess’s “I forget what you did it for” tell him?
facilitatorNotes: He reminds her that he can do it again; it is a quiet show of power. Her pretended forgetting tells him she is afraid of the subject, and she knows he sees it: he “seemed to know that and to play with it.” The conversation is a contest she is losing by politeness.
evidence: Except just that one night, you know———!
Oh, yes. But I forget what you did it for.
Why, it was to show you I could!

questions.prompt: In the churchyard Miles asks, “Does my uncle think what you think?” and then says he will bring him down. Why does this undo her? What has he understood?
facilitatorNotes: He has grasped that she has told the uncle nothing, and that the uncle’s coming is the thing she dreads. She sinks onto a tomb and, to answer, has to admit the uncle does not much care. Then he walks into church alone: the boy, not the governess, decides what happens next.
evidence: Does my uncle think what you think?
I don’t think your uncle much cares.
the boy said with extraordinary brightness and emphasis.

readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — the woman at the schoolroom table (Chapter XV)
readings.challenge: Trace the governess’s decisions in this chapter one by one, and what reverses each.
readings.focus: A flight that turns back at the sight of her predecessor in her own chair.
readings.context: The Turn of the Screw (1898), by Henry James, is the written account of a young governess, set down years afterwards, of her charge of two orphaned children, Miles and Flora, at Bly, a country house in England, for their uncle in London, who made her promise never to trouble him about them. She has come to believe that two figures she has seen at Bly are Peter Quint, the master’s valet, and Miss Jessel, the governess before her, both dead, and that the children secretly see and meet them; the housekeeper, Mrs. Grose, believes her. Miles has been expelled from school for a reason no one knows, and she has kept the matter from the uncle. Walking to church one Sunday, Miles asked when he would go back to school, said he wanted “my own sort,” and threatened to bring his uncle down himself, then walked into church alone, leaving her sitting on a tomb outside. To procrastinate is to put off; a conveyance, a carriage.
readings.contentNote: An apparition of a dead woman, “Dishonoured and tragic.”

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XV, the whole chapter; opens “The business was practically settled from the moment I never followed him. It was a…”; closes “…was nothing in the room the next minute but the sunshine and a sense that I must stay.”.

questions.prompt: What, in the governess’s account, did Miles “get out of” her in the churchyard? Why does she grant that he was “immensely in the right”?
facilitatorNotes: That she is afraid, above all of the question of his expulsion and what lies behind it, and that her fear can win him freedom. She admits his life with her is “unnatural for a boy” and that she has put off the uncle out of dread. It is a rare moment when she gives the boy’s view its due.
evidence: He had got out of me that there was something I was much afraid of
The boy, to my deep discomposure, was immensely in the right,
a life that’s so unnatural for a boy.

questions.prompt: Why does the governess decide to run away, and what stops her at the foot of the staircase?
facilitatorNotes: For the first time she wants to get away from Miles, and the empty Sunday house offers the chance. Collapsing on the bottom step, she remembers seeing “the most horrible of women” on that very spot, and the memory straightens her. Fear of the apparition gives her the strength to go on, which tells us something about what holds her at Bly.
evidence: For the first minute since his arrival I wanted to get away from him.
I could give the whole thing up—turn my back and retreat.
I had seen the spectre of the most horrible of women.

questions.prompt: Before she recognises the figure, the governess takes her for a housemaid writing to her sweetheart. Why might James have her appear first in that ordinary shape?
facilitatorNotes: She sits at the governess’s own table, with her pens and paper, weary, writing a letter, just as the governess will soon try to write one. She is less a monster than a double: a governess who loved unwisely and came to grief. Her look says that her right to the table is as good as the living woman’s.
evidence: I should have taken at the first blush for some housemaid
had applied herself to the considerable effort of a letter to her sweetheart.
her right to sit at my table was as good as mine to sit at hers.

questions.prompt: “I had the extraordinary chill of a feeling that it was I who was the intruder.” Why is this the most frightening moment in the chapter, and what does the governess do with the feeling?
facilitatorNotes: The apparition does not threaten; it claims the place, and for an instant the governess sees herself as the stranger. She answers by shouting at it, and the room is empty. Out of that protest comes her decision to stay. Students can debate whether she stays for the children or because the struggle has become hers.
evidence: the extraordinary chill of a feeling that it was I who was the intruder.
You terrible, miserable woman!
a sense that I must stay.

readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — “She suffers the torments” (Chapter XVI)
readings.challenge: Compare what the governess saw in the schoolroom with what she tells Mrs. Grose about it.
readings.focus: The governess decides to write to the uncle, and learns that Mrs. Grose cannot write.
readings.context: Recap: After Miles asked to go back to school, the governess stayed out of church, decided to leave Bly, and hurried back to the empty house to pack; in the schoolroom she found Miss Jessel sitting at her table, and her cry drove the figure away. She resolved to stay. “Swept and garnished” echoes a saying of Jesus about an empty house that evil spirits return to; the lost and the damned are souls in hell; the bailiff manages the estate.
readings.contentNote: The governess speaks of damnation and of a dead woman who wants a child.

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XVI, the whole chapter; opens “I had so perfectly expected that the return of my pupils would be marked by a…”; closes ““Well—tonight,” I at last answered; and on this we separated.”.

questions.prompt: The children say nothing about her absence from church. How does the governess read their silence, and Mrs. Grose’s?
facilitatorNotes: She had expected teasing; silence makes her suspect they have “bribed” Mrs. Grose. The truth, as Mrs. Grose tells it, is ordinary: they asked her to say nothing because the governess “would like it better.” Miles’s message, “We must do nothing but what she likes,” is either thoughtful or ironic, and her answer, “I wish indeed he would!”, shows which she hears.
evidence: I made sure they had in some way bribed her to silence;
We must do nothing but what she likes!
I wish indeed he would!

questions.prompt: Mrs. Grose asks, “Do you mean she spoke?” and the governess answers, “It came to that.” Look back at the scene in the schoolroom. Did Miss Jessel speak?
facilitatorNotes: In Chapter XV the figure said nothing; she only looked long enough “to appear to say” something. Now she has said that she suffers the torments of the lost and that she wants Flora. The story grows in the telling. Readers who doubt the governess count this as evidence; others say she is reporting what the look meant to her.
evidence: A talk! Do you mean she spoke?
It came to that.
She wants Flora.

questions.prompt: Why does the governess now decide to send for the uncle, and why does Mrs. Grose cry “Oh, no!” about the letter from Miles’s school?
facilitatorNotes: She will not let Miles think she is afraid; she will put the school’s letter before the uncle and refuse responsibility for a child expelled, she says, “For wickedness.” Mrs. Grose wants the uncle to come but not to see the letter, and turns pale: the fault is hers, she says, not his. Her reluctance hints at what she knew of Quint and the boy before the governess came.
evidence: he shall see he’s mistaken.
For wickedness. For what else—when he’s so clever and beautiful and perfect?
He didn’t really in the least know them. The fault’s mine.

questions.prompt: “How do you communicate?” “I tell the bailiff. He writes.” What does the discovery that Mrs. Grose cannot write change? Why does the governess’s next question sound sarcastic?
facilitatorNotes: Mrs. Grose cannot write, so any account of Bly must come from the governess’s pen, or from a bailiff who knows nothing. Her sarcastic “our story” points at the book we are reading: the only written version is hers. Mrs. Grose’s “Ah, Miss, you write!” gives her the authority, and the responsibility.
evidence: Remembering she couldn’t, I caught myself up.
I tell the bailiff. He writes.
And should you like him to write our story?
Ah, Miss, you write!

readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — the candle (Chapter XVII)
readings.challenge: Watch who controls the conversation at Miles’s bedside, and when control changes hands.
readings.focus: The governess begs Miles to let her save him; the answer is a gust of cold and darkness.
readings.context: Recap: The governess told Mrs. Grose that Miss Jessel appeared in the schoolroom and said she suffers the torments of the damned and wants Flora. She resolved at last to write to the children’s uncle, putting before him the letter that expelled Miles from school, and promised Mrs. Grose to write that night. The long dash ——— marks a sentence broken off. A sister of charity is a nursing nun; precocity, knowledge come too early.
readings.contentNote: A tense night scene between a governess and a boy in bed, ending in a shriek and darkness.

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XVII, the whole chapter; opens “I went so far, in the evening, as to make a beginning. The weather had changed back, a…”; closes ““It was I who blew it, dear!” said Miles.”.

questions.prompt: Miles calls to her through the door before she knocks. What does he say he lies awake thinking about? Is “this queer business of ours” a confession?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks of her, he says, and of “the way you bring me up. And all the rest!” She hears an admission that he knows about the dead. Read plainly, a boy kept under constant watch is describing the oddness of his own upbringing, and “you know, you know!” may mean only that she does.
evidence: I lie awake and think.
Well, I think also, you know, of this queer business of ours.
Why, the way you bring me up. And all the rest!

questions.prompt: The governess compares Miles to “some wistful patient in a children’s hospital” and herself to a nurse. What does the comparison show about how she sees her task?
facilitatorNotes: He is ill, with “the poison of an influence,” and she would cure him. At the end he looks at his raised hand “as one had seen sick children look.” The image is tender, and it also lets her treat what he says as symptoms rather than answers.
evidence: as appealing as some wistful patient in a children’s hospital;
the poison of an influence that I dared but half to phrase
holding up his hand to look at as one had seen sick children look.

questions.prompt: What does Miles want, in his own words, and why can’t she give it to him?
facilitatorNotes: To get away, “a new field,” and finally “To let me alone.” He wants his uncle to come and “settle things.” She cannot let him alone because, for her, turning away from him would be “to lose him.” Their wishes are exactly opposed.
evidence: I don’t—I don’t. I want to get away.
To let me alone,
to turn my back on him was to abandon or, to put it more truly, to lose him.

questions.prompt: “I just want you to help me to save you!” What happens next, and how many explanations does the text allow for the gust, the shriek and the dark?
facilitatorNotes: A blast of cold seems to shake the room, Miles shrieks, and the candle is out, yet the curtains have not moved and the window is shut. His shriek could be “jubilation or... terror.” His own explanation is simple: he blew it out. A ghost, a boy’s trick, or a frightened woman’s impression: James supplies each and confirms none.
evidence: I just want you to help me to save you!
a note either of jubilation or of terror.
the drawn curtains were unstirred and the window tight.
It was I who blew it, dear!

readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — David playing to Saul (Chapter XVIII)
readings.challenge: Follow the governess from the piano to the front door, and mark each step of her reasoning.
readings.focus: Miles plays the piano, Flora disappears, and the governess knows at once where she has gone.
readings.context: Recap: The governess began her letter to the uncle and, at Miles’s bedside, begged him to tell her what had happened at school; when she cried that she wanted to save him, a cold gust seemed to shake the room and the candle went out, and Miles said he had blown it. In the Bible the young David played the harp to calm King Saul’s dark moods. Luke is a manservant at Bly.

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XVIII, the whole chapter; opens “The next day, after lessons, Mrs. Grose found a moment to say to me quietly: “Have you…”; closes ““With them?” Oh, on this, the poor woman promptly joined me!”.

questions.prompt: The governess tells Mrs. Grose she has written, but the letter is still in her pocket. What does the delay suggest? What is odd about the children’s morning?
facilitatorNotes: She is still reluctant to summon the uncle; sending the letter means facing him. The children, meanwhile, are more brilliant and exemplary than ever, as if to smooth over the night’s “friction.” The governess reads the brilliance as strategy; it could also be children trying to please.
evidence: But I didn’t add—for the hour—that my letter, sealed and directed, was still in my pocket.
It was exactly as if they had both had at heart to gloss over any recent little friction.

questions.prompt: “All the justice within me ached for the proof that it could ever have flowered into an act.” What is the governess unsure of, and why does it matter to her?
facilitatorNotes: She is sure that Miles’s imagination has been opened to evil, but she cannot find a deed: what did he do to deserve expulsion? Justice needs an act, and she has only an influence. The gap between her certainty and her evidence is the problem she will press on to the end.
evidence: the enigma of what such a little gentleman could have done that deserved a penalty.
all the justice within me ached for the proof that it could ever have flowered into an act.

questions.prompt: The governess imagines a whole speech for Miles when he offers to play for her. Why put words in his mouth? Is the music a gift or a trick?
facilitatorNotes: The imagined speech, about true knights not pushing an advantage, is hers, not his; she reads his offer as a gentleman’s gesture. Then she “had forgotten” Flora. Afterwards she calls it “the most divine little way to keep me quiet,” and then “Infernal.” Students can argue for a kind boy playing music or a brother covering an escape.
evidence: David playing to Saul could never have shown a finer sense of the occasion.
I had only done something much worse—I had forgotten.
He found the most divine little way to keep me quiet while she went off.

questions.prompt: How does the governess know where both children are? What do Mrs. Grose’s questions show?
facilitatorNotes: Flora has gone out without a hat, and so, the governess says, does Miss Jessel; therefore Flora is with her, and Miles with Quint. Her calm surprises even her. Mrs. Grose asks practical questions (a hat, a coat, the letter) and is more afraid of being left in the house than of anything outside.
evidence: Isn’t that woman always without one?
Oh, he’s with Quint. They’re in the schoolroom.
My view, I was myself aware—and therefore I suppose my tone—had never yet reached so calm an assurance.

readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — across the lake (Chapter XIX)
readings.challenge: Notice how the governess turns each absence into proof.
readings.focus: The search for Flora at the lake, and the question that breaks the silence.
readings.context: The Turn of the Screw (1898), by Henry James, is the written account of a young governess, set down years afterwards, of her charge of two orphaned children, Miles and Flora, at Bly, a country house in England, for their uncle in London, who made her promise never to trouble him about them. She has come to believe that two dead servants, Peter Quint and Miss Jessel, the governess before her, haunt Bly and secretly possess the children; the housekeeper, Mrs. Grose, has believed her, though she has never seen them. Weeks ago the governess saw Miss Jessel across the lake at Bly while Flora played there, and was sure Flora saw her too and pretended not to. This afternoon, while Miles played the piano for her, Flora slipped away. Certain that she has gone to Miss Jessel, the governess left her letter to the children’s uncle on the hall table and rushed out, bareheaded, with Mrs. Grose. The long dash ——— marks a sentence broken off. A copse is a thicket.

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XIX, the whole chapter; opens “We went straight to the lake, as it was called at Bly, and I dare say rightly called,…”; closes “…too late now, and I brought the thing out handsomely. “Where, my pet, is Miss Jessel?””.

questions.prompt: The governess admits the lake may have been “less remarkable than it appeared to my untravelled eyes.” Why might she tell us this? Have you noticed other admissions like it?
facilitatorNotes: She confesses inexperience and a tendency to see things as larger than they are. It can make her seem honest, a narrator who corrects herself; it can also be a hint to the reader to discount her impressions. Earlier she wondered aloud whether she was “crazy.” James keeps giving the reader such openings.
evidence: may in fact have been a sheet of water less remarkable than it appeared to my untravelled eyes.
My acquaintance with sheets of water was small,

questions.prompt: When they cannot see the boat, the governess says: “Our not seeing it is the strongest of proofs.” What kind of reasoning is this? Is she right?
facilitatorNotes: Absence becomes evidence, as silence did earlier. This time she is right: the boat is hidden just where she guessed. Being right about the boat lends weight to her other claims, or shows only that she knows Flora’s habits. Her claim that Flora at such times is “an old, old woman” is of another kind and cannot be checked.
evidence: Our not seeing it is the strongest of proofs.
She’s not alone, and at such times she’s not a child: she’s an old, old woman.
we found the boat to be where I had supposed it.

questions.prompt: How does Flora greet them, and what do the fern and her question “Where are your things?” suggest?
facilitatorNotes: She smiles “as if her performance was now complete” and plucks a withered fern, as though that were her errand; the governess is sure she has come out of the thicket. Her first words notice that the women are bareheaded, a child’s sharp, ordinary observation, or a turning of the tables, since she has no hat either.
evidence: smiled as if her performance was now complete.
a big, ugly spray of withered fern.
Why, where are your things?

questions.prompt: Why does the governess finally say the name? What does the image of the cup “full to the brim” suggest about the moment?
facilitatorNotes: Flora’s “And where’s Miles?” is the jostle that makes the cup overflow: weeks of restraint spill out at once. The image suggests she is overwhelmed rather than deciding, yet she says she “brought the thing out handsomely.” Students can weigh whether this is courage, loss of control, or both.
evidence: the jostle of the cup that my hand, for weeks and weeks, had held high and full to the brim and that now, even before speaking, I felt overflow in a deluge.
Where, my pet, is Miss Jessel?

readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — “I see nobody. I see nothing.” (Chapter XX)
readings.challenge: Keep three pairs of eyes in view: where each looks, and what each says she sees.
readings.focus: The governess’s proof, and two witnesses who will not share it.
readings.context: Recap: Searching for Flora, the governess and Mrs. Grose found the boat hidden on the far side of the lake and the child on the bank beyond, smiling, a withered fern in her hand. When Flora asked where Miles was, the governess broke the long silence: “Where, my pet, is Miss Jessel?” The long dash ——— marks a sentence broken off. Reprobation is stern disapproval; pert, cheeky.
readings.contentNote: A frightened child turns against her governess, who is left alone weeping on the ground.

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XX, the whole chapter; opens “Just as in the churchyard with Miles, the whole thing was upon us. Much as I had made of…”; closes “…into a chair. We sat there in absolute stillness; yet he wanted, I felt, to be with me.”.

questions.prompt: The governess’s first feeling on seeing Miss Jessel is “joy at having brought on a proof.” Why joy? What does she feel toward the apparition?
facilitatorNotes: Proof that she is “neither cruel nor mad.” She even sends the figure “an inarticulate message of gratitude”: for a moment she is allied with the thing she calls a demon, since its appearance justifies her. The paradox shows how much she needs the visions to be real.
evidence: my thrill of joy at having brought on a proof.
she was there, and I was neither cruel nor mad.
an inarticulate message of gratitude.

questions.prompt: What does Flora’s face do, and why does it frighten the governess more than any ghost?
facilitatorNotes: Flora does not even glance toward the bank; she turns on the governess a hard, grave look that seems to “accuse and judge.” The child becomes the presence that makes her quail, and her beauty seems to vanish. A reader can see either a possessed child or a terrified one looking at the adult who frightens her.
evidence: an expression of hard, still gravity, an expression absolutely new and unprecedented and that appeared to read and accuse and judge me
she had turned common and almost ugly.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Grose asks, “Where on earth do you see anything?” How does her failure to see change the governess’s position? Does the governess accept it?
facilitatorNotes: Her one ally sees nothing, and the governess feels her “situation horribly crumble.” Yet within minutes she declares that if she had ever doubted, all doubt is gone, and explains Flora’s words as coming from “some outside source.” Every turn, even this one, becomes confirmation.
evidence: What a dreadful turn, to be sure, Miss! Where on earth do you see anything?
this hard blow of the proof that her eyes were hopelessly sealed
If I had ever doubted, all my doubt would at present have gone.

questions.prompt: “I think you’re cruel. I don’t like you!” Whose account of this scene do you find more convincing, Flora’s or the governess’s? Use the governess’s own words.
facilitatorNotes: Flora says she has never seen anything and asks to be taken away from the governess; the governess says the child speaks “under her dictation.” The governess reports Flora’s words in full, so the reader holds the evidence against her account too. Either judgement can be argued; the novel will not settle it.
evidence: I don’t know what you mean. I see nobody. I see nothing. I never have. I think you’re cruel. I don’t like you!
The wretched child had spoken exactly as if she had got from some outside source each of her stabbing little words,
I’ve done my best, but I’ve lost you. Good-bye.

readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — “I believe.” (Chapter XXI)
readings.challenge: Notice what Mrs. Grose says, what she hesitates to say, and what finally changes her mind.
readings.focus: Flora sent away, Mrs. Grose’s belief, and the letter that never went.
readings.context: Recap: At the lake the governess saw Miss Jessel on the far bank and called on Flora and Mrs. Grose to see her; Mrs. Grose saw nothing, and Flora, denying everything, begged to be taken away from the governess. Mrs. Grose took the child home; the governess lay weeping on the ground, then came back to find Flora’s things removed. That evening Miles sat with her by the fire in silence. The long dash ——— marks a sentence broken off. A chit is a pert child; town is London; to bring up the plumb is to haul up the weighted line that sounds a depth.
readings.contentNote: Flora is feverish and terrified, and is reported to use shocking language about her governess.

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XXI, the whole chapter; opens “Before a new day, in my room, had fully broken, my eyes opened to Mrs. Grose, who had…”; closes “…me on this, and I took her farewell. “I’ll save you without him!” she cried as she went.”.

questions.prompt: Flora is feverish and afraid, not of Miss Jessel but of her present governess. How does the governess explain this, and what does Mrs. Grose report?
facilitatorNotes: The governess pictures Flora resenting, like “some high little personage,” the slur on her truthfulness. Mrs. Grose says the experience has made her “quite old.” A plain reading sees a small child made ill by fear of the adult who frightened her; the governess sees a performance.
evidence: it was conspicuously and passionately against mine.
It has made her, every inch of her, quite old.
She resents, for all the world like some high little personage, the imputation on her truthfulness

questions.prompt: Why does the governess send Mrs. Grose and Flora away instead of going herself? What does she hope for from Miles?
facilitatorNotes: She reasons that her own leaving would look right but would abandon Miles; she will stay and win his confession, sure that “he wants to speak.” Her “remedy” is Mrs. Grose’s loyalty and Miles’s. Some readers admire her courage; others are alarmed that she arranges to be alone with the boy.
evidence: It’s you who must go. You must take Flora.
I do believe that—poor little exquisite wretch!—he wants to speak.
Get off with his sister as soon as possible and leave me with him alone.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Grose has “heard” horrors from Flora. Why does the governess cry “Oh, thank God!”? What does Mrs. Grose come to believe, and on what evidence?
facilitatorNotes: Flora’s shocking talk seems to prove that the child has been corrupted, and so justifies the governess. Mrs. Grose now says “I believe,” though she saw nothing at the lake; her evidence is a child’s language, which she admits she has “heard some of... before,” presumably in the days of Quint and Miss Jessel. A sceptical reader notes that a frightened child may say shocking things for other reasons.
evidence: From that child—horrors!
It so justifies me!
since I’ve heard some of it before!
I believe.

questions.prompt: The letter never left the hall table. What does Mrs. Grose conclude, and how does the governess answer? Why does her hope sound like a creed: “If he confesses, he’s saved”?
facilitatorNotes: Mrs. Grose decides that Miles took it and so must have been expelled for stealing. The governess is more cautious, then builds a new hope: the letter held so little that Miles is ashamed and ready to confess. Confession and salvation are religious words; she now sees herself as the boy’s confessor. Mrs. Grose’s farewell, “I’ll save you without him!”, is loyalty to her, not to the theory.
evidence: Your letter never went.
He stole letters!
If he confesses, he’s saved.
I’ll save you without him!

readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — alone with Miles (Chapter XXII)
readings.challenge: Watch the governess perform, first for the household and then for Miles, and ask whom she is convincing.
readings.focus: The last day begins with a solemn dinner for two.
readings.context: The Turn of the Screw (1898), by Henry James, is the written account of a young governess, set down years afterwards, of her charge of two orphaned children, Miles and Flora, at Bly, a country house in England, for their uncle in London, who made her promise never to trouble him about them. She has come to believe that two dead servants, Peter Quint and Miss Jessel, the governess before her, haunt the house and possess the children. Yesterday, at the lake, she named Miss Jessel to Flora; Flora denied seeing anything, turned against her, and has now been taken to her uncle in London by the housekeeper, Mrs. Grose, who came to believe the governess after hearing what the child said in the night. Mrs. Grose also told her that her letter to the uncle never left the hall table, and suspected Miles of taking it. The governess has stayed to have Miles to herself and win his confession. Weeks ago, at the dining-room window, she saw Quint look in. A joint is a roast; to dispense with attendance is to send the servants out.

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XXII, the whole chapter; opens “Yet it was when she had got off—and I missed her on the spot—that the great pinch really…”; closes “…of the waiter. He turned round only when the waiter had left us. “Well—so we’re alone!””.

questions.prompt: “It was precisely, in short, by just clutching the helm that I avoided total wreck.” What does the governess do to keep control after Mrs. Grose leaves? Whom is she performing for?
facilitatorNotes: She becomes “very grand and very dry,” parades the house looking ready for anything, and orders formal meals downstairs. The audience is the staring servants, Miles, and herself. Admitting that she “paraded with a sick heart,” she lets us see the performance and the fear beneath it.
evidence: I became, that morning, very grand and very dry.
So, for the benefit of whom it might concern, I paraded with a sick heart.
To mark, for the house, the high state I cultivated

questions.prompt: “Only another turn of the screw of ordinary human virtue.” Explain the phrase in its sentence. Why might James have taken his title from it?
facilitatorNotes: She keeps her balance by treating the horror as “nature,” only a harder test of ordinary goodness, one more turn of a screw tightening. The image suggests pressure, increasing strain, even an instrument of torture. As a title it fits the tale’s tightening suspense, and perhaps the governess’s tightening grip on the children.
evidence: only another turn of the screw of ordinary human virtue.
how my equilibrium depended on the success of my rigid will, the will to shut my eyes as tight as possible to the truth that what I had to deal with was, revoltingly, against nature.

questions.prompt: Miles asks about Flora: “Then why didn’t you get her off before?” How does the governess answer, and what does she mean by “The journey will dissipate the influence”?
facilitatorNotes: He asks sensible questions about a sudden illness and journey. She answers in double meanings: for him, the influence is Bly’s air; for her, Miss Jessel. Her aside, “oh, I was grand!”, mocks herself. Each speaker seems to understand more than he or she says.
evidence: Then why didn’t you get her off before?
The journey will dissipate the influence”—oh, I was grand!—“and carry it off.

questions.prompt: The chapter ends with an image: “some young couple who, on their wedding-journey, at the inn, feel shy in the presence of the waiter.” What does the comparison suggest about the governess and the boy? Why might it make readers uneasy?
facilitatorNotes: It catches the awkwardness of two people suddenly alone, with a joke at their own expense. It also casts a governess and a small boy as newlyweds, and Miles’s “Well—so we’re alone!” completes the picture. Some readers find it merely whimsical; others see in it the possessive intensity that drives the last chapters.
evidence: as some young couple who, on their wedding-journey, at the inn, feel shy in the presence of the waiter.
Well—so we’re alone!

readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — “But not now.” (Chapter XXIII)
readings.challenge: Read the dialogue twice: once for what is said, once for what each speaker is trying to make the other say.
readings.focus: A conversation like a duel, in which each fears for the other.
readings.context: Recap: Flora has gone to London with Mrs. Grose. The governess, alone at Bly with Miles, sat through a short, formal dinner with him in the dining room; the maid left them, and Miles, standing at the window where she once saw Quint look in, said: “Well—so we’re alone!” Wan means pale; cogitating, thinking hard; a portent, an omen; obtrusion, forcing in.

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XXIII, the whole chapter; opens ““Oh, more or less.” I fancy my smile was pale. “Not absolutely. We shouldn’t like that!”…”; closes “…yesterday afternoon, from the table in the hall, you took, you know, my letter.””.

questions.prompt: “Of course we have the others.” “We have the others—we have indeed the others.” What does each speaker mean by “the others”?
facilitatorNotes: Miles most likely means the servants: they are not quite alone. The governess, repeating it, means Quint and Miss Jessel. The whole exchange depends on one word meaning two things, and on each speaker suspecting the other’s meaning.
evidence: No—I suppose we shouldn’t. Of course we have the others.
We have the others—we have indeed the others,

questions.prompt: Watching Miles at the window, the governess feels “that I was not barred now” and that “it was positively he who was.” What does she think has changed? Why is it “a splendid portent” to her?
facilitatorNotes: She thinks Miles is looking for something he cannot see, for the first time shut out from the visitors as she has been. She rejoices at his anxiety because it means the influence is failing. Readers may find her pleasure in a child’s unease disturbing, which the narration does not hide.
evidence: the impression that I was not barred now.
Wasn’t he looking, through the haunted pane, for something he couldn’t see?
I found it a splendid portent.

questions.prompt: When does the governess first see fear in Miles, and what does she feel about what she is doing?
facilitatorNotes: He seems suddenly “afraid of me,” and she thinks that may be good. A moment later she feels “a perverse horror” and calls her pressing “an act of violence” on a helpless creature. She sees the harm clearly and continues. The image of fighters “not daring to close,” each afraid for the other, is both tender and ominous.
evidence: It was as if he were suddenly afraid of me—which struck me indeed as perhaps the best thing to make him.
To do it in any way was an act of violence,
But it was for each other we feared!

questions.prompt: Miles promises to tell her anything, “But not now,” and says he has to see Luke. Why does the governess say “his lies made up my truth”? What is her “very much smaller request”?
facilitatorNotes: The excuse is so thin that she takes it as a lie, and every lie confirms that he has something to hide, so it supports her view. She then asks, offhand over her knitting, whether he took her letter: a smaller question that may open the larger one. The chapter stops on it.
evidence: I mean I’ll tell you anything you like.
But, horrible as it was, his lies made up my truth.
if, yesterday afternoon, from the table in the hall, you took, you know, my letter.

readings.title: The Turn of the Screw — “Peter Quint—you devil!” (Chapter XXIV)
readings.challenge: Track what Miles can see and what the governess says she sees, line by line, to the last sentence.
readings.focus: The confession, the face at the window, and a death.
readings.context: Recap: Alone with the governess after dinner, Miles promised to tell her everything, but not now; he said he had to see Luke, a manservant. Before letting him go she asked one smaller thing: whether he had taken her letter from the hall table. A sentinel is a sentry; quenched, put out; his fall in the world, his loss of standing; “Stuff and nonsense!”, a scornful dismissal; dispossessed, freed from possession, and also deprived.
readings.contentNote: A governess struggles with a terrified child, and the novel ends with his death in her arms.

excerpt.locator: The Turn of the Screw, Chapter XXIV, the whole chapter, the end of the novel; opens “My sense of how he received this suffered for a minute from something that I can describe…”; closes “…held. We were alone with the quiet day, and his little heart, dispossessed, had stopped.”.

questions.prompt: As Quint’s face appears at the window, the governess decides “to keep the boy himself unaware.” Why? What does she call the struggle?
facilitatorNotes: She believes that if Miles does not see Quint while he confesses, the hold will break. She keeps him with his back to the window and calls it “fighting with a demon for a human soul.” The soul she holds is a sweating child: the language of spiritual battle meets a frightened boy’s body.
evidence: to keep the boy himself unaware.
It was like fighting with a demon for a human soul,
had a perfect dew of sweat on a lovely childish forehead.

questions.prompt: Miles admits he took and burned the letter, and that at school he “said things.” What do his answers suggest about why he was expelled? What thought frightens the governess most?
facilitatorNotes: He said things to a few boys “Those I liked,” they repeated them, and the masters heard; he thinks the things were “too bad” to write home. It is far less than she had imagined, and perhaps nothing worse than a boy’s forbidden talk. Her terror is that he may be innocent: “what then on earth was I?”
evidence: Well—I said things.
No—only a few. Those I liked.
if he were innocent, what then on earth was I?

questions.prompt: Miles asks “Is she here?” and then “It’s he?” Whom does he name, and whom does he call “you devil”? Does this prove he has seen them?
facilitatorNotes: He names Miss Jessel first, then Peter Quint, whom the governess has never named to him. “You devil” is most often taken as addressed to the governess, though it could be meant for Quint. Naming them shows that he knows of them; whether he has seen them, or learned the names from servants or from Flora’s scene, the text leaves open. The governess says the window was free to his eyes.
evidence: Is she here?
Peter Quint—you devil!
the window was still to his own eyes free,

questions.prompt: “We were alone with the quiet day, and his little heart, dispossessed, had stopped.” What are the possible meanings of “dispossessed”? Where does the last sentence leave the reader?
facilitatorNotes: Freed of possession, as in an exorcism, so the governess has won; or deprived, of life, of what sustained him, perhaps of the governess’s own grasp. Her claim of victory, “he has lost you for ever,” turns at once into loss. The novel ends with no outside witness and no explanation, only her account.
evidence: and his little heart, dispossessed, had stopped.
They are in my ears still, his supreme surrender of the name and his tribute to my devotion.
I have you,” I launched at the beast, “but he has lost you for ever!
